sections.0.body.0.t: A large share of any public application's traffic is automation: search engines and monitoring (useful), but also scrapers, credential stuffing, inventory hoarding and fake account creation. The defense is not blocking "bots", it is distinguishing intent and acting on abuse.

sections.1.body.0.t: Bot management solutions combine signals to produce a score per request. No signal is decisive alone, but together they separate traffic well:

sections.1.bullets.0.t: Network and TLS fingerprints: automation clients usually have signatures different from real browsers.

sections.1.bullets.1.t: Browser and behavior signals: JavaScript execution, movement, request cadence.

sections.1.bullets.2.t: Reputation and context: IP, ASN, client history, per-endpoint pattern.

sections.1.bullets.3.t: Verified bots: known crawlers (search engines, monitors) reliably identified and handled separately.

sections.2.body.0.t: The score blocks nothing by itself: policy defines the action per endpoint. A public catalog can tolerate a medium score, while login and checkout challenge or block. An example expression, in the style of Cloudflare rules:

sections.2.code.0.code.t:
# high automation risk on sensitive endpoints, ignoring verified bots
(cf.bot_management.score lt 30
 and not cf.bot_management.verified_bot
 and http.request.uri.path in {"/api/login" "/api/checkout"})
  -> action: Managed Challenge

sections.3.body.0.t: Classic challenges (CAPTCHA) punish real users. Modern managed challenges try to prove the client is a real browser without asking the user for anything, and only escalate to an interaction when doubt persists. The challenge is the step before blocking: it reduces false positives and still costs a lot for anyone automating at scale.

sections.4.bullets.0.t: Credential stuffing on login and password recovery.

sections.4.bullets.1.t: Scraping of prices, catalog or content.

sections.4.bullets.2.t: Mass account creation and promotion abuse.

sections.4.bullets.4.t: APIs: bots use the routes directly, so policy must also cover non-browser traffic.

short.t: separating legitimate automation from automated abuse

tagline.t: Not every bot is an enemy and not every human is legitimate. Bot management gives each request a trust score and lets policy decide what to do with it.
